name: Priya Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI firms, employers, unions, political parties and government; we don't sell or campaign. Your answers are confidential, including the parts you wouldn't say at work. What is a normal day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage four booking coordinators for a large venue company. We match room bookings, loading access and event crews across several halls. I have done it for thirteen years, hold a bachelor's degree and use AI planning tools every day, but I still walk the floor when a schedule looks wrong. I'm experienced at the job, not the company technical director.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and live with Niko, who makes paid bicycle deliveries. Our children are grown and have homes of their own. We have a mortgage; my manager pay is low here, nearby comparable jobs are scarce, and a roof leak left us two weeks of expenses in cash. Retirement is in sight, but neither of us has confirmed pension eligibility or amounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can still run the venue bookings desk through the first year. Yesterday two conferences were assigned the same loading bay, and our daily AI planner repeated the clash until my coordinator checked the floor map. A quiet technology year does not fix a cheap contract or our short cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my four coordinators to read the bay map before confirming an event. I'd tell the sales team that a booking is not ready until the access route is checked. I would use AI for a first schedule as I do now, then have a person sign the final plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have handled event changes for thirteen years, but I'm not a brilliant technical director. My manager wage is low and there are only a few comparable desks here. After our roof leak and repairs, Niko and I have two weeks of expenses saved; his paid bicycle deliveries vary with the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting Thursday I'll mark the three overlapping bay bookings on a paper floor map and ask each event lead to confirm the actual arrival time. I'll keep a human final check for bookings through 2027, and ask finance for the written margin on our largest venue contract before promising extra staff. I'll set aside 20 a week only if my pay and Niko's completed delivery income cover mortgage, food and roof instalments; I'll stop if his orders fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a contract mistake and our mortgage. A slow AI year still has bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened at the bay yesterday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The organiser's trucks had different arrival times in the email but the same slot on the AI schedule. I walked to the loading door with the floor manager, Jo, and found only one truck could turn there. A green schedule is no guarantee of a clear bay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who shares the roof bill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Niko and I both signed the repair plan and pay it from our combined income. Our grown daughter and son have their own flats and we do not put their salaries in our budget. I would ask them before relying on any help.

I'd tell sales that **access routes matter** as much as dates.
think: My **lower manager wage** and few nearby roles limit my options.
Two weeks cash and uneven delivery orders leave the **mortgage exposed**.
do: Mark **three overlapping bookings** on the floor map Thursday and confirm arrival times.
Keep a **human final check** on bookings and request the largest contract's written margin.
Save **20 weekly** only after mortgage, food and roof payments; stop if Niko's orders fall.
feel: I feel **anxious** about mistakes and the mortgage.

fieldNote: The floor manager found **one usable turning space** despite the green schedule.

New savings require **completed household income** after the roof payment.

Save 20 weekly after paid income covers mortgage, food, roof; stop if Niko orders fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A system that plans every room, contract and staffing rota would reach most of my desk. The bays still need people handling cables and trucks until robots can do that work, but digital room control and audio cues are thinking tasks too. I could have no coordinating hours even if the venue stays open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell event leads that I want one named human to approve any changed route. I'd ask the operations director for a closed rehearsal on last year's cancelled events and the floor manager's sign-off before a live schedule changes. I'd ask staff to record every missed access need during the rehearsal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI every day and can spot a bad prompt, but that is not a promise my wage survives. Niko's deliveries cannot cover our mortgage alone, and two weeks of cash would be gone fast. I would learn a new venue system if the company offered paid instruction, but I need real hours to pay the roof plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January I'll request director approval for a paid closed rehearsal using cancelled-event data only if the records officer permits that use; Jo, the floor manager, must verify the routes before we trust a result. If the director approves a successful test and the company provides paid instruction, I'll train on the new access console with Jo before any live assignment. I'll apply for posted event or facilities roles after checking wage and hours, leaving only for a signed offer that, with Niko's confirmed net deliveries, covers mortgage, food and roof instalments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my hours. Knowing the current tool well does not pay an instalment if my rota is cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let it change a live loading route?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if Jo has checked the rehearsal, the operations director signs the rule and an event lead can override a mistake. The records officer must permit the old event data before testing it. My own access password is not permission to reuse a client's file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if instruction is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep asking for a written staffing decision and keep the existing route check while I have hours. I cannot buy training with money set aside for the roof. A course without paid work attached would not solve our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 full AGI could negotiate bookings, set access routes and run digital lighting and sound cues. I expect my desk to lose most of its paid hours. Crews still carry stages and trucks until capable robots arrive around 2031; that does not guarantee me a crew vacancy or safe lifting work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the four coordinators to ask for written hours and redundancy terms. I'd tell Niko to hold off ordering a replacement delivery bike until we know our combined income. I'd tell clients where a human can challenge a wrong access plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large loss of my own wage in 2028, and two weeks cash will not bridge the mortgage and roof instalments. Niko's net delivery pay changes every month; it cannot replace my salary. I lie awake calculating which payment would bounce first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll request written hours and severance terms, and we'll defer the bike order before paying a deposit. If my desk closes after AGI arrives in 2028, I'll apply for posted nearby jobs only after checking actual hours, pay and any physical duties; I'll leave only for a signed offer whose wage plus Niko's confirmed net deliveries covers mortgage, food and roof instalments. If that combined income falls short, I'll check public assistance eligibility and apply only if we qualify; I'll speak to the lender before missing a mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. A glossy event can be sold without a person on my desk, but the roof bill is ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you join the stage crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can carry light signs but have never been trained to rig above people. I'd ask whether a paid opening exists, what the lifting involves and whether a trained supervisor can teach me on paid hours. Trucks and stage handling face capable robots around 2031, so I would not call it permanent shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move near the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They live in different cities and have their own costs. Niko and I would compare an actual job offer, housing and travel before discussing a move with them. We would ask if a short stay is possible, not presume a room.

say: I'd ask for **written hours and severance** for the team.
I'd tell clients how to **challenge access errors**.
I'd ask Niko to **delay the bike order**.
think: I expect **my wage to shrink** in 2028.
Two weeks cash and variable delivery pay cannot cover **mortgage and roof payments**.
do: Request **written pay terms** and defer the bike deposit.
Apply for **posted nearby work** after pay/hours/duty checks; accept signed wage plus Niko’s confirmed net deliveries covering mortgage, food, roof.
Check **public eligibility** and apply only if qualified; contact lender before arrears.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by likely wage loss and sleepless bill calculations.
S2.quote: A glossy event can be sold without a person on my desk, but the roof bill is ours.
fieldNote: A stage opening requires an **actual paid vacancy**, safe duties and trained supervision.
Digital venue control faces **2028 AGI**; physical staging faces 2031 robots.
A move requires **real work and housing**, not an assumed child's room.

steps.text: Apply after duty/pay/hours checks; accept signed wage plus Niko confirmed net deliveries covering mortgage/food/roof
Check public eligibility and apply only if qualified

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I might redesign the event handover so errors are visible and save beyond two weeks. The office still faces AGI in 2031 and the physical crews face robots around 2034. A longer runway gives me time to compare actual jobs, not a safe title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the director to publish a dated plan for which booking duties stay paid. I'd tell the team to keep a human route escalation for clients. I'd ask Niko to get his delivery receipts together so we can see real net income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can learn new controls quickly, but a new screen may make my post smaller. I don't know whether either pension will be payable at sixty-three or how much it would pay. Our mortgage and roof instalments need actual income, not a retirement date written on a calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'll request written pension eligibility dates and net estimates for both of us, then compare them with mortgage, food and roof costs. I'll apply for posted facilities coordination roles after checking actual pay and hours, and accept only a signed offer that meets those bills with Niko's confirmed net deliveries. If a real vacancy is posted and the venue offers paid supervised site time with funded safety training, I'll take a trial shift; I will not count its wages before an offer or ignore the 2034 robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a smaller post in 2031. I have time to make calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a facilities role pays less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the signed net wage and hours with our bills and Niko's completed delivery receipts before changing jobs. If the mortgage and roof instalments do not fit, I keep searching while my current wage lasts. I would not spend savings to make a weak offer look adequate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first pension question?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The provider must say whether we qualify at all and from which date. Then I need the net monthly amount, not a headline balance. Neither of us has those letters yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight in 2036, but I cannot assume we are eligible to retire. AGI could take the booking desk and digital event controls then; capable robots could handle much of the stage and loading work around 2039. Our grown children will have their own plans, not a standing obligation to pay our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the director to make changes to the access desk in writing. I'd tell Niko we need pension letters beside the loan statement. I'd tell clients that a route complaint needs a person to answer it, even if the schedule is automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years could let us pay down the roof repair and build cash if both incomes continue. My desk is still vulnerable in 2036, and I do not know whether real pension payments would cover the mortgage. Being quick with today's AI does not guarantee a paid place in tomorrow's system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'll request both providers' eligibility dates and net monthly amounts and keep the letters with our mortgage and roof schedule. I'll save 40 weekly toward a roof emergency fund only while my wage and Niko's completed delivery income pay mortgage, food and regular bills, stopping if his orders fall. In 2036 I'd reduce work only if confirmed eligible pension plus his actual net income covers those costs; otherwise I'll apply for posted paid work after checking wage, hours and duties, and accept only a signed offer that keeps the bills covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about an exposed desk and a thin reserve. Ten years is time to check, not a pension cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you sell the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would review a real sale price and the remaining mortgage before we even discuss it. Niko would need to agree, and replacement housing plus moving costs would have to fit our confirmed income. We cannot treat the roof bill as disappearing with the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your children pay that bill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They might help once if asked, but they have rent and families of their own. I would speak to them only after Niko and I know the actual shortfall, and rely on help only if they freely offer it. Our children’s kindness is not a line in our mortgage budget.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the bookings desk could lose most of its hours before we rebuild cash. Niko's variable deliveries would not cover the mortgage and roof instalments alone. Written hours terms, a real paid offer at workable hours and verified pension figures would help; a route-appeal contact matters for customers too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who is standing at the loading bay when the schedule changes. Jo can see a truck blocking an exit before a screen does. I want the route approver named in writing, especially when the room has already been sold.

headlineQuote: I want the route approver named in writing, especially when the room has already been sold.

She uses **AI planning daily** but checks access routes on the floor with staff.
Low manager pay, scarce nearby roles, Niko's variable deliveries and **two weeks cash** expose their mortgage.
She asks for **written pay terms** and real pension figures before relying on a new role or retirement.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove most booking hours while the mortgage and roof repair still need paying.
